title: Lightning Talk

speakers.name: Kyle Easterly
speakers.affiliation: Co-Founder and CEO, Delve Group, Anchorage, Alaska (video description and title slide)

thesis: People outside the field understand AI poorly, so Delve Group built a glass-topped, fully offline GPU machine called LOAD (Local Offline AI Demonstration) that shows how AI works on real hardware, and he urges the audience to build something similar to explain AI to their neighbours.
summary: Kyle Easterly of Delve Group in Anchorage, Alaska, says the customers his AI deployment software company meets in oil and gas, healthcare and telecom see AI as a chat box and a data center. To fix that, he and an intern named Brian built LOAD, a rackmount machine laid flat on a table with a plexiglass lid, running models entirely offline. A 3D digital twin of every part lets visitors tour the machine with a Stream Deck or by voice. Easterly describes the build: two GPUs, an EPYC CPU, 256 GB of ECC memory, a custom water loop, and open models served with vLLM, assembled in about a month using SSDs he already owned. It debuted on Sep 28, 2026 and has since been shown at a leadership summit, a university computer science class and industry trade shows, and he hopes to take it to the state capital. Demos include watching a small model pick its next word layer by layer, a fleet of 21 agents building a town in the style of the Stanford generative agents paper, handwritten fuel tickets turned into structured data, and a live fine-tune in which a Llama model learns who built it. He says hardware failures happened in public and treats that as part of the lesson. He closes by asking the audience to help the people around them understand AI. The talk has no security content.
argument: Non-specialists see AI only as a chat box and a data center, and lack a basic model of how it works.
Showing the real hardware, running offline, in front of people makes AI concrete and removes the sense that it lives somewhere else.
Interactive demos such as watching a model pick words or learn a fact in a live fine-tune build intuition about training and inference.
Showing failures in public helps people learn to trust the machine.
The audience understands AI better than almost anyone and should build something similar and explain it to their neighbours.

claims.claim: LOAD, a single offline box with two GPUs and no internet connection, can run the full demo set including a 21-agent fleet using Gemma 4.
claims.evidence: Description of the machine and demos; slide lists 1 box on a 24-inch-deep table, 2 GPUs visible through the lid, 0 internet connections.

claims.claim: A live LoRA fine-tune on about 100 facts changes a 1B-parameter Llama's answer to 'Who built you?' within 15 to 30 seconds on one GPU.
claims.evidence: Slide figures; in speech he said the full training takes about a minute and a pause at 10 steps shows hallucinated creators such as Google or California universities.

claims.claim: The build went from parts to public use in about a month, with the first commit on the night of Sep 27 and public debut on Sep 28.

The machine had several hardware failures in public: a hang at 1:05 AM before the debut, a full power-off during the debut session, a weak memory cell caught by ECC, and a GPU that stopped answering on Oct 11 (Xid 119), replaced by an RTX 3090.
claims.evidence: Failure slide with a photographed crash console.

claims.claim: Pausing training early and asking the model who built it shows its answer drifting away from Meta towards Alaska and finally to Delve Group.
claims.evidence: Easterly's description of the demo as a teaching device.

claims.claim: Claude was used heavily: to make the slide deck minutes before the talk, to write the overnight first version of the app, and to read 96 photos to update the digital twin after the cooling refit.

slide_only: Title slide: LOAD, Local Offline AI Demonstration, with the line 'We put AI on a folding table in Alaska so people could finally see it'; labelled [un]prompted II Turbo Talk.
Idea slide: 'AI is a file running on a chip. Not a place.'

Build slide: RTX A6000 48 GB plus RTX 3090 24 GB; AMD EPYC 7443 24 cores; 256 GB ECC; 8 SATA SSDs in RAID 5 plus 4 NVMe scratch; custom water loop 360 mm copper radiator; ~1 kW peak estimate; Ubuntu, vLLM, open models, .NET app; 'Built like a production server, not a gaming PC.'

Timeline: Aug to Sep design and build; Sep 27 night first commit; Sep 28 1:05 AM rig hangs, back at 6:09; Sep 28 public debut at AI in Alaska Leadership Summit; Oct 1 and early Oct Top 49ers Luncheon and UAA CS classroom visit; Oct 11 to 12 GPU dies, RTX 3090 replaces it; Oct 16 to 19 cooling refit; Oct 27 onward telecom, mining, resources and utility shows.

Demos slide: Inside the AI, Agent Fleet, Paper logs; also on the deck: Teach (live fine-tune), Dispatch (voicemail to work order), What if (plain-English planning), Code Gen (2019 to 2026 models write Breakout), Ask the machine (voice), image and video generation.
Failure slide: 'Showing what broke is how people learn to trust the thing.'
Refit slide: before, a manifold on the side wall with every block in parallel; after, distribution blocks on a brace and one loop in series.
Digital twin slide: built from vendor CAD, taken apart by hand in a Quest 3 headset; 'still a work in progress'.

Closing slide quote dated Sep 16, 2026: 'This machine will end up being a pivotal moment in many people's journeys to understand AI.' with points: if people can see it they can reason about it; plain words, measured numbers, nothing hidden; build one and explain it to your neighbours.
demos: Inside the AI: shows a small model picking its next word layer by layer.
Agent Fleet: 21 agents message each other and build a town, then live in a town built by the first fleet.
Paper logs and voicemail triage: handwritten fuel tickets become structured data; voicemail becomes a work order.
Live fine-tune: a Llama model asked who built it says Meta, then after fine-tuning says Delve Group, Kyle and Brian; stopping early shows hallucinated creators.
VR: a Quest 3 headset lets a visitor remove a GPU from the digital twin while the software shuts that GPU off in the real machine. These were described, not shown live.

takeaways: On one team's experience, with no measured effect, build a tangible offline demo where non-technical stakeholders struggle with AI literacy.
As an approach to test, show training and inference on real hardware, including failures, to build trust with customers and policymakers.
Run demos on offline local models. Customer data is then not sent to external services, which matters for sensitive sectors.
limits: Easterly said he had seen the slides only once, and that he had more slides than time.
He said the digital twin is still a work in progress and the machine had a fried GPU and other hardware faults.
No evidence was presented on whether the demo changes audience understanding.
critique: The educational effect of the demo was not measured.
The fine-tune timing differs between speech (about a minute, and about 3 minutes per visitor) and the slide (15 to 30 seconds), so the two figures differ.
The demos use small models whose behaviour was not compared with frontier systems.

signal.reason: The talk presents an offline GPU demo machine for AI literacy, with its hardware specification and build timeline, and has no security content or measured results on audience understanding.

caveats: The captions say Dove Group; the slide says Delve Group, and this record uses the slide.

The speaker said an A6000 GPU died and that he fried one GPU; the slide says the GPU that stopped answering was replaced by an RTX 3090 and lists an A6000 plus a 3090 in the build, and this record uses the slide.
Slides skip numbers (3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14, 17 appear), so the deck was shown at pace and not all slides are captured.
Easterly said Brian was a University of Alaska Anchorage intern; no surname was given.
